description:
We are a team of motivated high school students from Bulgaria, guided by our programming teacher. With experience in C#, JavaScript, web development, and teamwork, we are passionate about technology and innovation.

Our goal is to learn, create, collaborate, and have fun while building something meaningful together!
summary:
Kids hear that astronauts are going to Mars and the Moon, but nobody shows them the hard part. On a real outpost there is never enough power, food, crew time and radiation protection all at once, and today's choice can cost you days later.

The Impossible SOLution is a free browser game for ages 7–12, in English and Bulgarian, with no login. Players run a base on Mars or the Moon and face real events, like the 20 May 2024 solar storm, when NASA's Curiosity measured radiation on Mars at more than 50 times its usual level. At the end, a domino chain shows which early choice caused each result.

Every number is real NASA data or clearly labelled as a game number. No choice is free, and saved data is never called live.
details:
Why we built it

Space missions run on trade-offs, but school teaches space as facts to memorise. We wanted kids to make the decisions mission planners make and see the results.

What it does and how it works

  • Three campaigns on real data:
    • The Storm Season: Mars, 5 sols, easy.
    • Dust Season: Mars, 6 sols, medium.
    • South Pole Outpost: the Moon, 5 days, hard.
  • Every day plays differently: choosing a landing site, wiping dusty solar panels by hand (which costs radiation dose), picking an upgrade, radioing Earth, a crew dilemma, driving the rover, watching the sky.
  • Real storms: three solar storms Curiosity measured on Mars (2017, 2021, 2024), each with its NASA DONKI event ID shown in the game.
  • Live data where it exists: "Ask Earth" uses today's real Earth–Mars light delay from the Deep Space Network (about 11 minutes right now). "Today's real Sun" checks current DONKI forecasts aimed at Mars, and says honestly when the Sun is quiet.
  • Domino chain: the final screen links each outcome back to the choice that caused it.
  • Replayable: each run has a number you can replay, there's a Daily mission, and the storm strikes on a different day each time.
  • Honest data: every reading is labelled LIVE or SAVED DATA. A "Where our numbers come from" screen lists each real fact with its source and date checked, plus every made-up game number. The game also works offline.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Kids practise systems thinking: power, food, air and shielding all depend on each other.
  • They meet real science (light delay, radiation dose, dust on solar panels), with every term explained in short sentences.
  • Teachers can use it in class straight away: free, two languages, no login, runs on phones, and a teacher mode opens every campaign.
  • It's accessible: big tap targets, full keyboard and touch play, screen-reader labels, and reduced-motion support.

Tools and technologies

  • Code: TypeScript, React, Vite, Zustand, zod, i18next (EN/BG).
  • Testing: Vitest, Testing Library, MSW, plus headless-Chrome scripts that play every campaign to the end.
  • Hosting: Vercel, with a small serverless proxy that keeps our NASA API key secret and caches the data.
  • Data: NASA DONKI, OSDR RadLab (Curiosity RAD, LRO CRaTER), InSight, Opportunity, Curiosity REMS, Mars Trek, Moon Trek, Artemis candidate landing regions, Deep Space Network, and CSA.
  • Art and fonts: pixel art drawn as code with the open-source tool pxl, Nunito and Pixelify Sans fonts (OFL licence).
  • Music composed by Viktor Devanatan, one of the game's developers, from Sofia, Bulgaria.
  • AI: we used Claude Code as a coding assistant. Every use is listed in our AI usage log and was reviewed by the team.

What makes it creative

  • Most space games show resources as numbers. Ours shows what each choice causes, through the domino chain.
  • Every disaster is a real, dated event with its NASA ID, not a random one.
  • The radio delay is measured live, so the game changes with where Mars actually is.
  • One engine runs every campaign, so a new mission is just new data.

What we considered

  • Age 7–12 reading level: short sentences, and every term explained when it first appears.
  • Scientific honesty: every number checked against its NASA source. For example, the 2024 flare is described as "estimated X12 or larger", not a flat "X12".
  • Demo reliability: it falls back to bundled data when the network fails.
  • Privacy: no accounts, no tracking, and no faces or voices of minors.
